title: Insert Interval
directAnswer: The input is already sorted and non-overlapping, so you don't need to re-sort. Walk the list once in three phases: copy every interval that ends before the new one starts, merge every interval that overlaps the new one into a single expanding interval, then copy the rest. That's O(n) time, O(n) output.

remember.pattern: Three-phase linear sweep over sorted, non-overlapping intervals
remember.formula:
# 1) before:   while end_i < newStart:        keep interval
# 2) overlap:  while start_i <= newEnd:        new = [min(starts), max(ends)]
# 3) after:    append merged new, then keep the rest
rules: The input is **already sorted by start and non-overlapping** — re-sorting is the rookie move that throws away the O(n) you were handed.
Two intervals overlap iff `a.start <= b.end AND b.start <= a.end`. Touching endpoints (`[1,2]` and `[2,3]`) count as overlapping for this problem.
While merging, grow the new interval in place: `newStart = min(newStart, cur.start)`, `newEnd = max(newEnd, cur.end)`.
Append the merged interval **once**, after the overlap phase ends — not inside the loop.
Three sequential `while` loops over the same index `i` is cleaner than one loop with branchy `if/else` — say that out loud.
whenToUse: Input intervals are already sorted and disjoint, and you insert/merge one new range
You want O(n) without paying for a sort
Calendar / booking 'add this slot and merge conflicts' framing
A single new interval, not a batch — batch turns it into Merge Intervals
antiSignals: Intervals are unsorted → sort first, then it's Merge Intervals (LC 56)
You must insert many intervals → re-merge the whole set instead
You only need to know IF it overlaps, not the merged result → a single boolean scan
Endpoints are exclusive (`[1,2)` doesn't touch `[2,3)`) → flip the comparison to strict `<`
remember.takeaway: When an interval list arrives pre-sorted, the sort is a gift — spend it on a single linear pass. Insert Interval is the cleanest example of the three-phase 'before / overlap / after' sweep that also powers Merge Intervals and most calendar problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you notice the input is already sorted and exploit it for O(n), instead of blindly appending the new interval and re-running a full sort-and-merge.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Re-sorting the array (paying O(n log n) for nothing), or getting the overlap condition wrong so touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] don't merge.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the three phases before coding, name the overlap test precisely (start <= end on both sides), and mention you could binary-search the insertion point to cut the 'before' scan to O(log n).

problemStatement:
You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]` represent the start and end of the iᵗʰ interval, and `intervals` is **sorted in ascending order by startᵢ**.

You are also given an interval `newInterval = [start, end]` that represents the start and end of another interval.

Insert `newInterval` into `intervals` such that `intervals` is still sorted in ascending order by `startᵢ` and `intervals` still does not have any overlapping intervals (merge overlapping intervals if necessary).

Return `intervals` **after the insertion**.
constraints: intervals is sorted by startᵢ in ascending order
understanding: You're handed a clean, sorted, gap-respecting timeline and one new event to drop in. Anything strictly to the left or right of the new event is untouched; anything that touches or overlaps it gets fused into one bigger interval. Return the timeline still sorted and still disjoint.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input guaranteed sorted and non-overlapping?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole point. It lets us skip the sort and run a single O(n) pass.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] count as overlapping?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: For this problem, yes — they should merge into [1,3]. If endpoints were exclusive we'd use strict inequality instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the new interval land before everything, after everything, or fill a gap with no overlap?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: All three are valid. The three-phase structure handles 'no overlap' naturally — the overlap loop just runs zero times.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can intervals be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — if intervals is empty we simply return [newInterval].

examples.explanation: [2,5] overlaps [1,3] (2 ≤ 3), so they merge into [1,5]. [6,9] starts after 5, untouched.
[4,8] overlaps [3,5], [6,7], and [8,10], fusing them into [3,10]. [1,2] is before, [12,16] is after.
Nothing to merge with — the new interval is the whole answer.

approaches.name: Append, Sort, Merge — Reuse Merge Intervals
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it as the 'I could just reduce this to a problem I already know' fallback — then point out it wastes the sorted input.
hints: You already know how to merge a list of unsorted intervals. Can you turn this problem into that one?
Push newInterval onto the list, sort everything by start, then do the standard sweep-merge.
It works and it's easy to reason about — but ask yourself what the 'already sorted' guarantee was for.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The sort dominates at O(n log n); the merge sweep is O(n). The sort is pure waste here because the input minus the new interval was already ordered.
approaches.explanation:
Treat the problem as Merge Intervals with one extra element. Append `newInterval` to the list, sort the whole thing by start, then sweep left-to-right fusing any interval whose start is ≤ the previous interval's end.

**Why reach for this first.** If you've already solved Merge Intervals, this is the lowest-risk path: you're reusing a routine you trust instead of writing new index gymnastics. In an interview it's a perfectly good thing to *say* — 'the safe version is to append and re-merge' — because it shows you can decompose a new problem into a known one.

**Why it's not the answer they want.** The prompt hands you a list that is *already sorted and already non-overlapping*. Sorting it again throws that guarantee in the bin and pays `O(n log n)` for information you were given for free. The interviewer chose 'sorted input' on purpose — it's a flashing sign that an `O(n)` solution exists. Use this as the warm-up, then beat it.
approaches.insight: Reducing a new problem to a solved one is a real skill — but only when you can't do better. Here the sorted-input guarantee is the tell that a linear solution is reachable, so this O(n log n) version is a stepping stone, not the destination.

pitfalls: Mutating the input `intervals` array in place while sorting — copy first.
Using `<=` instead of `<` in the disjoint test merges touching intervals (here that's desired, but be deliberate).
Forgetting this re-sort is the whole inefficiency — don't present it as the final answer.

approaches.name: Three-Phase Linear Sweep (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'before / overlap / after' — three sequential loops over one index, no sort.
hints: The list is already sorted and disjoint. What can you copy verbatim before you even look at the new interval?
Split the work into three contiguous regions: intervals entirely before the new one, intervals that overlap it, and intervals entirely after.
In the overlap region, keep expanding newInterval: newStart = min(newStart, cur.start), newEnd = max(newEnd, cur.end). Append it once when overlapping stops, then copy the rest.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each interval is visited by exactly one of the three loops, doing O(1) work — so O(n) time. Output holds up to n+1 intervals → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the list with a single index `i`, in three sequential phases.

**Phase 1 — before.** While the current interval ends *strictly before* the new interval starts (`intervals[i][1] < newStart`), it can't possibly overlap, so copy it to the result untouched and advance. Because the input is sorted, once this stops, every remaining interval starts at or after this point.

**Phase 2 — overlap.** While the current interval starts *at or before* the new interval ends (`intervals[i][0] <= newEnd`), it overlaps the (possibly already-grown) new interval. Don't append these — instead absorb them: `newStart = min(newStart, intervals[i][0])` and `newEnd = max(newEnd, intervals[i][1])`. The new interval swells to cover the whole overlapping run. When the loop ends, append the merged new interval exactly once.

**Phase 3 — after.** Everything left starts strictly after the merged interval ends, so copy the remaining intervals verbatim.

**Why three loops beat one branchy loop.** You *could* do this in a single loop with `if before / elif overlap / else after`, but the three-phase version makes the invariant obvious: each phase owns a contiguous slice of the sorted input, and the index only moves forward. It's easier to reason about and easier to get right under interview pressure.
approaches.insight: The sorted, disjoint guarantee means the answer is naturally partitioned into three contiguous blocks: untouched-left, one fused middle, untouched-right. The only 'work' is fusing the middle — and fusing is just running min over starts and max over ends. Spot that partition and the code writes itself. If you wanted to shave the 'before' phase to O(log n), binary-search for the first interval whose end ≥ newStart — but the copy still makes the whole thing O(n), so it rarely matters.

dryRun.intro: Three phases over index i. Watch newInterval grow from [4,8] to [3,10] as it absorbs the overlapping run.

code.python:
def insert(self, intervals: list[list[int]], newInterval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    res: list[list[int]] = []
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    new_start, new_end = newInterval
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < new_start:
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= new_end:
        new_start = min(new_start, intervals[i][0])
        new_end = max(new_end, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    res.append([new_start, new_end])
    while i < n:
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    return res

java.explanation: Phase 1 — interval ends before new one starts → cannot overlap, copy it.
Phase 2 — interval starts at or before new end → overlaps, absorb instead of copy.
Grow the new interval's right edge to swallow this overlapper.
Append the fully-merged interval ONCE, after the overlap run ends.

diagrams.title: Three phases over the timeline
diagrams.caption: Each cell is an interval. Phase 1 copies (dim), phase 2 absorbs (highlight), phase 3 copies the tail.

edgeCases.behavior: Before-phase copies nothing (1's end 3 ≥ 2); overlap absorbs [1,3] → [1,5]; [6,9] copied after → [[1,5],[6,9]].
Before-phase copies [1,5] (5 < 6); overlap runs zero times; append [6,8] → [[1,5],[6,8]] (a gap-filling insert).

pitfalls: Using `<=` in phase 1's test makes a touching interval skip the merge — phase 1 must be strict `<`.
Appending the new interval inside the overlap loop produces duplicates — append once after the loop.
Forgetting phase 3 drops every interval after the merge region.

commonMistakes: Re-sorting the already-sorted input, paying O(n log n) for nothing.
Getting the overlap condition wrong so touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] don't merge.
Appending the new interval inside the overlap loop instead of once after it.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Re-sorting the input you were handed sorted
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The prompt guarantees the list is already sorted by start. Sorting again costs O(n log n) and signals you missed the entire reason the input was specified that way.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
all_iv = intervals + [newInterval]
all_iv.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])  # O(n log n) — wasted

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Appending the new interval inside the overlap loop
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Each overlapping interval would push a copy of the (still-growing) new interval, producing duplicates. The merged interval is finalized only after the overlap run ends.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= new_end:
    new_end = max(new_end, intervals[i][1])
    res.append([new_start, new_end])  # appends every iteration
    i += 1
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= new_end:
    new_start = min(new_start, intervals[i][0])
    new_end = max(new_end, intervals[i][1])
    i += 1
res.append([new_start, new_end])  # once

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong inequality in the before-phase
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Phase 1 must stop on the first interval that could touch the new one. Using `<=` lets a touching interval (end == newStart) slip into the copy-as-is phase and never merge.

patternNote: Three-phase interval sweep on sorted input. Recognise it whenever you insert/merge into an already-ordered, disjoint interval list. Same 'before / overlap / after' partition powers Merge Intervals and most calendar-booking problems.
